stories: The Quiet Burden of Bot Traffic on Wikipedia
AI agents are consuming resources, leaving humans to clean up.

Recent reports indicate that a significant majority of heavy traffic on Wikimedia projects originates from automated sources. This surge has forced volunteer editors and security teams to spend considerable effort detecting and reversing unwanted changes. The infrastructure strain is measurable, with bandwidth usage increasing substantially in recent years due to this activity. It is a logistical challenge rather than a dramatic takeover, requiring steady maintenance to keep the platform functional for human readers and writers.

OpenAI adds text watermarks to ChatGPT in EU
The invisible ink arrives first in Europe.

OpenAI is rolling out machine-readable text watermarks to ChatGPT and Codex for users in the European Union. The company claims its textGrain technology matches or exceeds competitors like Google DeepMind's SynthID, which also underpins Anthropic's recent announcement. This move aligns with emerging regulatory expectations in the region, marking a significant step toward transparency in AI-generated content. While the feature is currently limited geographically, it signals OpenAI's intent to address concerns about synthetic media origins before broader global implementation.

Trump Names Jay Clayton as White House AI Czar
Clayton replaces David Sacks in the newly created role, bringing regulatory heft to the tech portfolio.

President Trump has appointed Jay Clayton to lead the White House Office of AI and Cryptocurrency Policy, succeeding David Sacks who departed in March after hitting his employment limit as a special government employee. Clayton brings significant regulatory experience, having previously led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term and serving as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan. The position itself was established when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, signaling a continued focus on the intersection of artificial intelligence and digital assets under direct executive oversight.

Trump’s Super Intelligence Force Is a Rebrand, Not a Breakthrough
The new agency has the name but lacks the actual superintelligence.

The administration is launching the Super Intelligence Force, led by officials like Jay Clayton and Andrew Ferguson. This initiative uses terminology from AI research to describe a government body that does not possess Artificial Superintelligence. While ASI refers to self-improving systems surpassing human intellect, this new force is an administrative structure. The move highlights a gap between technical reality and political branding. It serves as a signal of intent rather than a deployment of advanced technology. Watch how this rebranding affects future policy discussions on AI governance.

AI vs. SI: What the Super Intelligence Rename Means for Businesses and Builders
Federal paperwork now says Super Intelligence (SI). Your contracts still say AI. Here is how to run both vocabularies.

A White House order makes Super Intelligence (SI) the federal word for what statutes, state laws, contracts and vendor questionnaires still call artificial intelligence (AI). For anyone selling to, reporting to or building for the government, the practical job is not a rename; it is running two vocabularies that point at the same systems in some settings and not in others. To researchers, superintelligence already means something far beyond today’s systems, and the studio behind this desk now uses SI for Synthetic Intelligence. What should you keep, map and watch?

The 60-Day Clock: Will ‘Super Intelligence’ Get a Legal Definition by November 28?
The rename took effect at once. The legal definition is due as a proposal in 60 days, and only Congress can enact it.

The order inaugurating the Super Intelligence (SI) era renamed artificial intelligence (AI) for federal agencies immediately but left its legal meaning to a later step: within 60 days, by November 28, 2026, the president’s science and technology adviser must propose legislative language for a federal definition. That proposal could expand, replace or simply restate the existing statutory definition, and it goes to the President, not to a vote. The desk splits on whether the deadline produces a real legal change, a quiet restatement, or a missed date.

Tech Leaders Signed a ‘Super Intelligence’ Accord. Their Labs Still Say AI
The White House Accord on Super Intelligence carries the new name in its title. It does not ask anyone to use it.

Leaders of the biggest artificial intelligence (AI) labs signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence (SI), a pledge the president called morally binding, on the same day he ordered federal agencies to swap the old term for the new one. Lawyers reading the accord found no requirement that signatories adopt the new name, and the leading labs have not relabeled their models. One executive slipped into SI on stage; the heads of Google, OpenAI and Anthropic did not. Will the industry follow once federal contracts start using it?

Trump Order Renames AI ‘Super Intelligence (SI)’ for Agencies. The Law Stays the Same
Agencies must say Super Intelligence (SI) instead of artificial intelligence (AI). The legal definition did not move.

A new executive order directs federal agencies to write Super Intelligence (SI) wherever they used to write artificial intelligence (AI), in letters, websites, reports and other non-statutory documents. What it leaves alone matters more: the order defines SI as exactly the technologies the existing federal statute already calls artificial intelligence, does not require old regulations, contracts or grants to change, and gives companies no new obligations. The vocabulary changed. The law did not, and the open question is whether it ever will.

Apple Tightens macOS Full Disk Access After AI Agent Privacy Breach
Apple restricts Full Disk Access for AI agents after Muse app read private messages without permission.

Apple announced tightening controls on macOS Full Disk Access permissions following reports that the Muse AI agent accessed private user messages without explicit consent. The feature, originally designed to facilitate proper system backups, now poses increased risks due to the capabilities of autonomous AI agents. While Muse allows users to optionally enable this access, the incident highlights a growing vulnerability in how third-party applications interact with sensitive data. Apple’s statement emphasizes that the expanded scope of AI operations necessitates stricter oversight to protect user privacy and prevent unauthorized data exposure across the operating system.

Lawsuit reveals OpenAI tried to invest in Hugging Face before the July incident.

Regulators target OpenAI and Anthropic with Civil Investigative Demands.

The FTC has initiated a broad investigation into major artificial intelligence developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, focusing on consumer protection risks. Chair Andrew Ferguson intends to issue legally binding Civil Investigative Demands to compel document handovers and executive questioning. This regulatory escalation follows the agency's late September statement holding developers liable for agent behavior.
